events.title: Earliest Human Activity Traces
events.description: Archaeologists have discovered evidence of possible human activity on the Comoros Islands dating back to around 2000 BCE. These early traces include simple stone tools and fire remains, suggesting early humans may have intermittently visited or briefly inhabited these islands. The volcanic islands' geographical features provided early explorers with freshwater sources and abundant marine resources. Human activity from this period remains mysterious but provides important clues for understanding Comoros' prehistory.

events.title: Early Austronesian Settlement
events.description: The earliest inhabitants of the Comoros Islands likely came from Austronesian peoples who migrated from Southeast Asia via Madagascar. Archaeological evidence shows early settlers brought outrigger canoe technology, agricultural knowledge, and Austronesian languages. These early migrants established small agricultural communities on the islands, cultivating taro, bananas, and coconuts. The strategic location of Comoros made it an important waypoint on Indian Ocean trade routes.

events.title: Early Pottery Culture
events.description: A distinctive pottery-making tradition emerged on the Comoros Islands, combining Austronesian and African techniques. Archaeological excavations reveal pottery from this period featuring simple geometric decorations, used for cooking and storage. Pottery styles show cultural connections with Madagascar and the East African coast. These early settlers also began utilizing the islands' abundant volcanic rock for making tools and building materials.

events.title: Fishing and Maritime Development
events.description: Early Comorian inhabitants developed sophisticated fishing and maritime techniques. They used outrigger canoes and sailing vessels to navigate between islands, catching tuna, sharks, and other marine life. Coral reefs provided abundant marine resources including shellfish, octopus, and sea turtles. Maritime skills enabled islanders to maintain contact with Madagascar and the East African coast, engaging in small-scale trade and cultural exchange.

events.title: Agricultural Technology Advances
events.description: Comorian inhabitants began developing more complex agricultural systems, including terrace farming and irrigation techniques. They cultivated various crops including taro, yams, bananas, breadfruit, and coconuts. The fertile volcanic soil was well-suited for agricultural development. Inhabitants also began raising poultry, especially chickens, which became an important protein source. Agricultural development supported population growth and more complex social organization.

events.title: Bantu Migration
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples from the East African mainland began migrating to the Comoros Islands. These migrants brought iron-working technology, new agricultural methods, and Bantu languages. The Bantu mixed with earlier Austronesian inhabitants, creating Comoros' unique cultural fusion. Pottery and iron artifacts from this period have been discovered on Anjouan and Mohéli, proving Bantu influence.

events.title: Iron Age Begins
events.description: With the arrival of Bantu peoples, Comoros entered the Iron Age. The use of iron tools revolutionized agricultural production, making forest clearing and cultivation more efficient. Iron weapons and tools also transformed social structures, promoting the emergence of more complex political organizations. Blacksmiths gained special status in society, their skills viewed as mysterious and powerful forces.

events.title: Early Trade Networks
events.description: Comoros began participating in broader Indian Ocean trade networks. Islanders engaged in small-scale trade with merchants from the East African coast, Madagascar, and possibly Arab traders. Comoros exported coir fiber, tortoiseshell, spices, and marine products in exchange for pottery, beads, cloth, and metal goods. These early trade contacts laid the foundation for later large-scale commercial activities.

events.title: Pre-Islamic Religious Beliefs and Customs
events.description: Before the arrival of Islam, Comorian inhabitants practiced animism and ancestor worship. They believed spirits (djinns) inhabited volcanoes, forests, and oceans, requiring appeasement through rituals and offerings. Tribal elders and shamans presided over religious ceremonies including harvest celebrations, coming-of-age rituals, and funerals. Elements of these pre-Islamic beliefs later merged with Islam, forming Comoros' unique religious culture that continues to influence local customs today.

events.title: Arab Traders Arrival
events.description: Arab merchants began frequently visiting the Comoros Islands, establishing trading posts. They brought Islam, Arabic language, and new trade networks. Comoros became an important trade hub connecting East Africa, Arabian Peninsula, Persia, and India. Arab merchants traded spices, ivory, slaves, and tortoiseshell. This period marked the beginning of Islamization of Comoros, with Arab culture having profound influence on the islands.

events.title: Spread of Islam and Mosque Construction
events.description: Islam gradually spread throughout the Comoros Islands as Arab and Persian Muslim merchants intermarried with local inhabitants, facilitating religious conversion. The first wooden mosques were established on each island, becoming religious and social centers of communities. Quranic teachers began teaching Arabic and Islamic doctrine. Although Islamization was a gradual process, by the end of the 9th century many coastal communities had embraced Islamic faith while retaining some indigenous customs.

events.title: Shirazi Persian Settlement
events.description: Muslim merchants and migrants from Shiraz, Persia established permanent settlements in Comoros. The Shirazi brought Persian architectural styles, Islamic scholarly traditions, and commercial expertise. They established early sultanates on Grande Comore, introducing Islamic law and administrative systems. Shirazi tradition claims many Comorian noble families originated from Persia, becoming an important part of local elite identity.

events.title: Formation of Islamic Sultanates
events.description: Independent Islamic sultanates began forming on each Comoros island. Each island developed its own political structure, ruled by sultans assisted by Islamic scholars and noble councils. These sultanates controlled trade, collected taxes, and maintained relations with other Muslim polities in the Indian Ocean. Mosques and Quranic schools were established on each island, with Islam becoming central to social and political life. The Comorian language (Shikomori) began developing, blending Bantu, Arabic, and Persian elements.

events.title: Rise of Stone Architecture
events.description: Stone architecture began appearing in Comoros, marking significant advances in building technology and social wealth. Wealthy sultans and merchants constructed mosques, palaces, and residences using coral stone and volcanic rock. These buildings blended Swahili, Arab, and Persian architectural styles, forming a unique Comorian architectural tradition. The emergence of stone architecture reflected prosperity from Indian Ocean trade and the cultural aspirations and political power of the Comorian elite.

events.title: Indian Ocean Trade Prosperity
events.description: Comoros reached its peak position in Indian Ocean trade networks. The islands became a key transit point connecting the East African Swahili coast, Madagascar, Arabian Peninsula, Persian Gulf, and India. Comoros exported spices (especially cloves and cinnamon), tortoiseshell, coir fiber, and slaves, importing textiles, ceramics, metalwork, and luxury goods. Muslim merchant communities prospered on each island, building stone mosques and palaces. Architectural remains from this period, such as the Domoni Mosque on Anjouan, showcase Comoros' wealth and cultural achievements.

events.title: Madagascar Connections
events.description: Comoros maintained close trade and cultural ties with neighboring Madagascar. Frequent movement of people and goods between the two promoted cultural exchange. Rice from Madagascar became an important import for Comoros, while Comorian Islamic culture influenced northwestern Madagascar. Some Comorian sultans established marriage alliances with Malagasy rulers. This cross-channel interaction shaped the languages, customs, and social structures of both regions.

events.title: Anjouan Sultanate Zenith
events.description: The Sultanate of Anjouan (Ndzuwani) became the most powerful political entity in Comoros. The Anjouan sultan controlled important ports and trade routes, accumulating great wealth. Sultan palaces and mosque architecture displayed refined Islamic art and architecture. Anjouan became an Islamic scholarly center, attracting scholars from East Africa and the Arab world. The sultanate maintained a sophisticated administrative system including taxation, judiciary, and military organization.

events.title: Portuguese Explorers Arrive
events.description: Portuguese explorers discovered the Comoros Islands on their route to India. The Portuguese mapped the islands and recorded Comoros' geography and society in their navigation logs. Although the Portuguese did not establish permanent colonies in Comoros, their arrival marked the beginning of European contact with Comoros. The Portuguese occasionally stopped in Comoros for fresh water and food supplies, but mainly focused on controlling Mozambique and other parts of the East African coast.

events.title: Sultanate Competition and Division
events.description: The four main Comoros islands (Grande Comore, Anjouan, Mohéli, and Mayotte) each developed independent sultanates competing for trade control and political influence. Conflicts and alliances between islands constantly shifted, causing political instability. Each sultanate tried to attract foreign merchants and establish trade monopolies. This division weakened Comoros' collective strength against external threats, but also promoted the development of unique cultural and political traditions on each island.

events.title: English East India Company Trading Post
events.description: The English East India Company established a temporary trading post on Anjouan, attempting to monopolize Comoros trade. The English signed trade agreements with local sultans, exchanging textiles and metalwork for food and supplies. However, due to disease, local resistance, and economic difficulties, the English presence was brief. This attempt showed European powers' interest in Comoros' strategic location, but also proved local rulers' ability to maintain independence.

events.title: Dutch and English Merchants
events.description: Ships from the Dutch East India Company and English East India Company began regularly visiting Comoros, seeking supplies and trade opportunities. European merchants were interested in Comoros' spices, tortoiseshell, and slaves. Comorian sultans established trade relations with European merchants but remained vigilant to maintain their independence. The arrival of Europeans increased Comoros' importance in Indian Ocean trade, but also brought new competition and conflicts.

events.title: Madagascar Pirate Base
events.description: European pirates began using Comoros and neighboring Madagascar as bases to raid merchant ships in the Indian Ocean. Some pirates established relationships with Comorian sultans, providing protection money in exchange for sanctuary. Pirates brought European goods and wealth, but also violence and instability. Some pirates even married local women and integrated into Comorian society. Pirate activity during this period made Comoros a notorious region in the Indian Ocean.

events.title: French Exploration
events.description: French explorers and merchants began showing interest in Comoros, viewing it as a strategic point on the route to India and the East. The French conducted geographical surveys and trade exploration in Comoros, laying the foundation for future colonial expansion. France established initial contact with Comorian sultans, exchanging gifts and building diplomatic relations. This marked the beginning of French influence expansion in the Indian Ocean region, eventually leading to Comoros being incorporated into the French colonial empire.

events.title: Slave Trade Expansion
events.description: Comoros became an important center of the Indian Ocean slave trade. Slaves from the African mainland were transported to Comoros, then transshipped to Madagascar, Réunion, Mauritius, and the Arabian Peninsula. Comorian sultans and nobles profited greatly from the slave trade, which became a pillar of the islands' economy. Slaves were also used locally in Comoros for agricultural labor and domestic work. The slave trade brought wealth but also created social inequality and moral issues, affecting Comorian social structure.

events.title: Malagasy Sakalava Invasion
events.description: The Sakalava Kingdom army from Madagascar invaded Mayotte Island, conquering the local sultanate. Sakalava ruler Andriantsoly established control over Mayotte, introducing Malagasy political and cultural influence. This invasion changed Mayotte's demographic composition and cultural characteristics, making it different from other Comorian islands. Sakalava rule lasted for decades until French colonizers arrived.

events.title: Malagasy Raids on Grande Comore
events.description: Sakalava forces from Madagascar raided Grande Comore (Ngazidja), plundering villages and capturing slaves. These raids caused significant destruction and casualties, weakening the Grande Comore sultanate's power. Comorian rulers sought external assistance to resist Malagasy threats, creating opportunities for later French intervention. Conflicts between Madagascar and Comoros reflected power struggles and territorial disputes in the western Indian Ocean region.

events.title: French Annexation of Mayotte
events.description: French naval officer Passot signed a treaty with Mayotte Sultan Andriantsoly, ceding Mayotte Island to France. France paid 1,000 silver dollars as compensation and promised to protect the sultan. This was France's first step in establishing colonial rule in Comoros. Mayotte became a French strategic base in the Indian Ocean, used to control the Mozambique Channel and protect French interests in Madagascar and Réunion. This annexation aroused vigilance and resistance from other Comorian islands.

events.title: French Colonial Administration Established
events.description: France established formal colonial administrative institutions in Mayotte, appointing a governor and officials to manage island affairs. France introduced legal systems, taxation, and land ownership systems, changing traditional social structures. France encouraged French settlers and Creoles from Réunion to migrate to Mayotte, establishing plantations for sugarcane and vanilla. Mayotte began separating from other Comorian islands, developing a distinct French colonial culture.

events.title: French Penetration of Other Islands
events.description: France began exerting influence on Anjouan, Mohéli, and Grande Comore through trade agreements, military threats, and diplomatic means. French merchants established trading posts on each island, and French warships regularly patrolled Comorian waters. France exploited conflicts between islands and internal divisions within sultanates to gradually expand its influence. Comorian sultans faced pressure from French colonial expansion but still tried to maintain independence and traditional power.

events.title: Mohéli Sultan Treaty with France
events.description: The Sultan of Mohéli signed a protection treaty with France, recognizing French suzerainty in exchange for protection. This further expanded French influence in Comoros. Mohéli became a French protectorate, with French advisors participating in island administration and economic affairs. This treaty was part of France's strategy to gradually annex the entire Comoros archipelago, achieving colonial control through diplomatic means rather than direct military conquest.

events.title: Anjouan Becomes French Protectorate
events.description: Under internal conflicts and external pressure, the Sultan of Anjouan accepted French protection. France promised to protect the sultan from hostile forces in exchange for control over island affairs. France established administrative institutions in Anjouan, introducing French law and economic systems. Anjouan's spice plantations expanded under French management, especially ylang-ylang (perfume ingredient) production became an important economic activity.

events.title: Grande Comore Sultan Resistance
events.description: Sultan Said Ali of Grande Comore (Ngazidja) attempted to resist French colonial expansion, seeking alliances with Zanzibar and the Ottoman Empire. Said Ali was a powerful ruler who unified multiple small sultanates on Grande Comore, establishing a relatively strong central authority. He refused to sign protection treaties, trying to maintain Comorian independence. However, facing French military and economic pressure, his resistance ultimately proved unsustainable.

events.title: Complete French Annexation of Comoros
events.description: France formally annexed the entire Comoros archipelago, including Grande Comore. Sultan Said Ali was forced into exile, and France established direct colonial rule. Comoros became part of the French colonial empire, administratively subordinate to the Governor of Madagascar. France abolished the traditional sultanate system, introducing French administration, law, and education systems. This marked the end of Comorian independent history and the formal beginning of the colonial period.

events.title: Colonial Economic System Established
events.description: France established a colonial economic system in Comoros, focusing on developing spice plantations, especially vanilla, ylang-ylang, cloves, and cinnamon. French companies obtained large land concessions, establishing large plantations. Locals were forced into low-wage plantation labor, and traditional subsistence agriculture was marginalized. Comoros' economy became completely dependent on agricultural exports to France and European markets. This monoculture structure made Comoros vulnerable to international market fluctuations.

events.title: World War I Impact
events.description: During World War I, Comoros as a French colony was mobilized to support the war effort. Hundreds of Comorians were conscripted into the French army, many dying on European battlefields. Comorian agricultural products were used to support France's war economy. The war caused economic hardship and social upheaval, but also exposed some Comorians to the outside world, beginning to question the legitimacy of colonial rule.

events.title: Colonial Education and Islamic Schools
events.description: France established a colonial education system in Comoros, teaching French language and culture, attempting to assimilate the local population. However, traditional Islamic Quranic schools continued operating, preserving Arabic language and Islamic knowledge. This created a dual education system: French schools trained colonial administrative elites, while Islamic schools maintained religious and cultural traditions. This educational division reflected cultural tensions in Comorian society under colonial rule.

events.title: Infrastructure Modernization Begins
events.description: The French colonial government began limited infrastructure development in Comoros. Roads were built on main islands connecting coastal villages with interior plantations, improving transportation. Moroni port facilities were improved to facilitate export of spices and other agricultural products. However, infrastructure investment primarily served colonial economic interests rather than local people's needs. Electricity supply was limited to administrative centers and European residential areas, with most Comorians still relying on traditional lifestyles.

events.title: Consolidation of Spice Plantation Economy
events.description: By the late 1920s, Comoros' colonial economy was entirely dependent on spice plantations. Ylang-ylang became the most important export product, with Comoros supplying most of the world's ylang-ylang essential oil used in the perfume industry. Vanilla, cloves, and cinnamon were also important export commodities. French companies controlled plantations and export trade, with local farmers receiving meager incomes. This economic structure made Comoros extremely vulnerable to international market price fluctuations, laying the groundwork for future economic fragility.

events.title: Great Depression Impact
events.description: The global Great Depression of the 1930s severely affected Comoros' export-oriented economy. Spice prices plummeted, plantation income sharply declined, and unemployment rose. Many Comorians fell into poverty, forced to return to subsistence agriculture. The French colonial government cut public spending, exacerbating economic difficulties. The economic crisis of this period exposed the fragility of the colonial economic system, triggering discontent with French rule.

events.title: World War II Period
events.description: During World War II, Comoros initially remained loyal to the Vichy French government. In 1942, British forces occupied Comoros to prevent Japanese expansion in the Indian Ocean. After the war, Comoros returned to Free French control. During the war, Comoros' economy further deteriorated, with material shortages and inflation intensifying. The war experience made Comorians more aware of colonial rule's injustice, laying the foundation for post-war nationalist movements.

events.title: French Overseas Territory Status
events.description: After the war, Comoros became a French Overseas Territory (Territoire d'outre-mer), gaining limited autonomy and representation in the French Parliament. Comorians obtained French citizenship and could elect representatives to the French National Assembly. This status change gave Comoros more political participation opportunities, but actual power remained in the hands of French-appointed governors. This marked a transition from direct colonial rule to a more complex colonial relationship.

events.title: Comoros Separated from Madagascar
events.description: Comoros was administratively separated from Madagascar, becoming an independent French Overseas Territory with its own administrative institutions. The capital was established in Moroni (Grande Comore). This change gave Comoros greater administrative autonomy, but also meant Comoros had to bear more administrative costs itself. The separation reflected cultural and political differences between Comoros and Madagascar, and Comorian elites' demands for greater autonomy.

events.title: Political Awakening and Early Organization
events.description: After World War II, signs of political awakening appeared in Comoros. French-educated Comorian elites began organizing discussion groups and cultural associations to debate autonomy and reform issues. Though small in scale and monitored by colonial authorities, these early organizations laid foundations for later political movements. Some Comorians began working in France and other African colonies, encountering anti-colonial ideas and nationalist movements, bringing these ideas back to Comoros.

events.title: Nationalist Movement Emergence
events.description: Nationalist movements began emerging in Comoros, demanding greater autonomy and eventual independence. Inspired by the Asian-African decolonization wave, Comorian intellectuals and political activists organized political parties and social movements, challenging French colonial rule. Key political figures like Said Mohamed Cheikh began advocating for Comorian self-determination. This period marked the awakening of Comorian political consciousness and the beginning of the independence movement.

events.title: Loi Cadre and Local Assembly
events.description: France enacted the Loi Cadre (Framework Law), providing more local autonomy to overseas territories including Comoros. Comoros established a local assembly, giving local representatives more power to participate in decision-making. Though limited, this reform marked an important shift in colonial governance. Comorian politicians began debating local policies in the assembly, gaining experience for future autonomous government. However, real power remained in the hands of the French governor.

events.title: French Community Referendum
events.description: In de Gaulle's French Community referendum, Comoros voted to remain within the French system, becoming an autonomous territory of the French Community. The referendum results showed Comorian hesitation about complete independence, partly due to economic dependence and concerns about post-independence instability. However, this referendum also gave Comoros greater internal autonomy, including its own parliament and government. This was an important step toward Comorian independence.

events.title: Internal Autonomy
events.description: Comoros gained greater internal autonomy, establishing its own government and parliament responsible for most internal affairs. France retained control over defense, foreign affairs, and monetary policy. Said Mohamed Cheikh became President of the Comorian Government, leading the autonomous government. During this period, Comoros began developing its own political institutions and civil society, preparing for future independence. However, political divisions between islands and economic challenges also began emerging.

events.title: Economic Modernization Attempts
events.description: The Comorian autonomous government attempted to promote economic modernization and diversification in the early 1960s. The government encouraged development of fisheries, tourism, and small industries to reduce dependence on spice exports. However, due to funding shortages, technical limitations, and resistance from vested interests, these efforts had limited success. France still controlled Comoros' major economic sectors, and local entrepreneurs lacked capital and technology. The failure of economic modernization highlighted the rigidity of the colonial economic structure and the difficulties of Comorian development.

events.title: Social Change and Women's Status
events.description: In the mid-1960s, Comorian society began experiencing slow social changes. More women received education, and some educated women began working in government departments and education. However, traditional Islamic customs and patriarchal systems still dominated social life. The expensive traditional 'Grand Mariage' wedding continued as a symbol of social status, imposing heavy economic burdens on families. The younger generation began questioning these traditions, but change progressed slowly.

events.title: Student Movement and Independence Demands
events.description: Comorian students and intellectuals launched movements demanding complete independence. Inspired by the 1968 global student movement and African decolonization processes, Comoros' younger generation more radically opposed French rule. Protests and strikes erupted on each island, demanding France recognize Comorian independence rights. These movements increased pressure on France, accelerating the independence process.

events.title: Population Growth and Migration Pressure
events.description: In the early 1970s, Comoros faced rapid population growth, pressuring limited resources and employment opportunities. Many young Comorians began migrating to mainland France, Réunion, and Madagascar seeking work opportunities. Diaspora communities began forming, with remittances becoming an important component of the Comorian economy. Population pressure intensified competition for land and resources, also strengthening demands for economic development and political change.

events.title: Independence Negotiations Begin
events.description: The Comorian government and France began formal negotiations on independence. Comorian leader Ahmed Abdallah pushed the independence agenda, but faced French resistance and internal divisions. Mayotte's residents, mainly Christians and pro-French, opposed independence, wanting to remain with France. This division foreshadowed the future Mayotte problem. The independence negotiation process was long and complex, reflecting conflicts of interest within Comoros and with France.

events.title: Independence Referendum
events.description: Comoros held an independence referendum, with 94.5% of voters overall supporting independence. However, Mayotte's voting results showed 63.8% opposed independence, wanting to remain with France. This divided result triggered a constitutional crisis: the other three Comorian islands insisted on overall independence, while Mayotte demanded to remain separately with France. France exploited this division, supporting Mayotte's separatist position, laying the foundation for future territorial disputes.

events.title: First Coup d'État
events.description: Just one month after independence, Comoros experienced its first coup. Ali Soilih overthrew President Ahmed Abdallah, establishing a radical socialist regime. Soilih was a young revolutionary influenced by Maoism and African socialism. He promised thorough social reforms, breaking the power of traditional elites. This coup opened an era of political instability in Comoros, with coups becoming the norm in Comorian politics.

events.title: Comoros Unilateral Declaration of Independence
events.description: The Comorian Parliament under President Ahmed Abdallah unilaterally declared independence, including all four islands including Mayotte. The newly independent Comorian state faced enormous challenges: economic backwardness, inadequate infrastructure, weak administrative capacity, and the Mayotte separation issue. France refused to recognize Comorian sovereignty over Mayotte, continuing to control the island. Comoros joined the United Nations and Organization of African Unity, gaining international recognition, but the Mayotte issue became a lasting dispute.

events.title: Soilih Radical Reforms
events.description: Ali Soilih implemented radical social and economic reforms: abolishing traditional sultan titles and noble privileges, promoting women's liberation, lowering marriage age, banning expensive traditional weddings, establishing youth militia organizations, and pursuing secularization policies limiting Islamic religious influence. These reforms challenged Comoros' traditional social structure and Islamic values, arousing strong opposition from conservatives and religious leaders. Soilih's rule was chaotic and authoritarian, the economy deteriorated, and social divisions intensified.

events.title: Mayotte Second Referendum
events.description: Under French organization, Mayotte held a second referendum, with 99.4% of voters choosing to remain with France. France subsequently established Mayotte as a French 'special collectivity' (collectivité territoriale). The Comorian government and Organization of African Unity strongly protested, considering this a violation of territorial integrity principles and UN resolutions. The UN passed multiple resolutions recognizing Comorian sovereignty over Mayotte, but France refused to comply. The Mayotte issue became the core dispute in Comoros-France relations.

events.title: Bob Denard Coup
events.description: French mercenary Bob Denard led a coup, overthrowing the Ali Soilih regime and restoring Ahmed Abdallah as president. Soilih died mysteriously shortly after the coup, officially said to be killed while trying to escape, but widely believed to be murdered. Denard became the behind-the-scenes manipulator of Comorian politics, controlling the Presidential Guard and security apparatus. This coup marked the beginning of foreign mercenary involvement in Comorian politics, also reflecting France's continued influence on Comoros.

events.title: Abdallah Authoritarian Rule
events.description: After Ahmed Abdallah restored the presidency, he established authoritarian rule, relying on Bob Denard's mercenaries to maintain power. Abdallah abolished Soilih's radical reforms, restored traditional Islamic and social order, and rebuilt relations with France and Arab countries. He renamed Comoros the 'Federal Islamic Republic of the Comoros,' emphasizing Islamic identity. However, his rule was corrupt and suppressed dissent, the economy remained difficult, and political opposition was repressed.

events.title: Abdallah Assassination
events.description: President Ahmed Abdallah was assassinated in the presidential palace, officially attributed to rebels, but Bob Denard and his mercenaries were widely suspected of involvement. Abdallah's death triggered a political crisis and power vacuum. Denard attempted to control the situation but faced international pressure. France and South Africa intervened, forcing Denard to leave Comoros. Supreme Court Chief Justice Said Mohamed Djohar became interim president. This assassination exposed the violence and instability of Comorian politics.

events.title: Multi-party Democratic Transition
events.description: Under international pressure and domestic demands, Comoros began transitioning to a multi-party democratic system. A new constitution allowed multi-party competition and regular elections. Said Mohamed Djohar was elected president in the 1990 elections. However, the democratic transition was not smooth, with electoral fraud allegations, political violence, and military intervention continuing to plague Comoros. Political parties were mainly based on island and personal loyalties rather than ideology, leading to political fragmentation and instability.

events.title: Denard Coup Again
events.description: Bob Denard again led a mercenary coup, overthrowing President Djohar. Denard claimed to be invited by Comorian opposition, but actually acted for his own economic and political interests. France strongly opposed, sending troops to arrest Denard and repatriate him to France. Djohar was restored to the presidency, but his power was weakened. This incident showed Comoros' vulnerability to foreign intervention and France's continued influence in Comorian affairs.

events.title: Political Chaos and Economic Crisis
events.description: Comoros fell into serious political chaos and economic crisis. Frequent coups, government changes, and political violence destroyed economic development and social stability. International aid decreased, investors withdrew, and unemployment soared. Comoros became one of the world's poorest countries, heavily dependent on foreign aid and diaspora remittances. Infrastructure was backward, education and healthcare systems collapsed. The crisis of this period highlighted the failure of Comorian state-building and lack of governance capacity.

events.title: Anjouan and Mohéli Separatist Crisis
events.description: Anjouan and Mohéli islands declared independence from Comoros, demanding to rejoin France or become independent states. The separatist movement was driven by dissatisfaction with central government corruption and neglect, and envy of Mayotte's economic benefits from remaining with France. Anjouan and Mohéli's separation seriously threatened Comoros' territorial integrity and state survival. The central government attempted to restore control through negotiation and military means, but with limited effect. This crisis exposed deep divisions between Comorian islands and the fragility of national identity.

events.title: Military Coup and Azali's Rise
events.description: Army Chief of Staff Azali Assoumani launched a military coup, overthrowing interim President Tadjidine Ben Said Massounde. Azali promised to restore order, resolve the separatist crisis, and hold democratic elections. He suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament, and established military rule. Azali attempted to negotiate with Anjouan and Mohéli separatists, but negotiations progressed slowly. The international community, especially the African Union and Francophonie, pressured for a peaceful resolution to the crisis.

events.title: African Union Mediation
events.description: The African Union (formerly Organization of African Unity) actively mediated the Comoros crisis, organizing negotiations among all parties. South African President Thabo Mbeki served as chief mediator, promoting dialogue between the Comorian government and Anjouan and Mohéli separatists. After difficult negotiations, parties agreed to establish a new federal system, giving each island greater autonomy. This mediation process showed the role of African regional organizations in resolving member state conflicts, also reflecting the regional impact of the Comoros problem.

events.title: Fomboni Accord
events.description: Under African Union mediation, Comorian parties signed a peace agreement in Fomboni, Madagascar, establishing a new federal system. The agreement stipulated Comoros be renamed the 'Union of the Comoros' (Union des Comores), composed of three autonomous islands (Grande Comore, Anjouan, Mohéli), each with its own president and parliament. The Union presidency would rotate among the three islands, each term four years. This innovative power-sharing arrangement aimed to balance interests between islands and prevent future separatist crises.

events.title: New Constitution Referendum
events.description: Comoros held a new constitution referendum, approving the federal system established by the Fomboni Accord. The new constitution received 75% support, providing a legal basis for Comoros' political reorganization. The constitution stipulated the Union president would be responsible for foreign affairs, defense, and monetary policy, while island presidents would be responsible for internal affairs like education, health, and agriculture. This complex power distribution aimed to satisfy each island's autonomy demands while maintaining national unity. However, power division between Union and island governments remained contentious in practice.

events.title: Azali Elected Union President
events.description: In the first election under the new constitutional framework, Azali Assoumani was elected President of the Union of the Comoros. As a candidate from Grande Comore, Azali defeated his opponent in the second round. He promised to consolidate peace, promote economic development, and improve relations with the international community. Azali transformed from military ruler to elected president, but his governing style remained authoritarian, facing opposition criticism. This election marked Comoros' transition from crisis to relative stability.

events.title: Anjouan Separatist Crisis Again
events.description: Anjouan island President Mohamed Bacar refused to recognize the Union government's authority, effectively declaring independence. Bacar was a former military officer who controlled Anjouan's security forces and refused to participate in Union presidential elections. He held his own election in Anjouan, declaring his re-election as island president, but the election was not internationally recognized. This new separatist crisis threatened the achievements of the Fomboni Accord, drawing attention from the Union government and African Union.

events.title: Sambi Elected Union President
events.description: According to the rotation system, a candidate from Anjouan should be elected Union president. Ahmed Abdallah Mohamed Sambi won the election, becoming the new Union president. Sambi was an Islamic scholar and businessman, called a 'moderate Islamist.' He promised to resolve the Anjouan crisis, fight corruption, and promote economic development. Sambi's election showed the rotation system's operation, but he faced the daunting task of confronting Anjouan separatists.

events.title: African Union Military Intervention in Anjouan
events.description: After diplomatic means failed, the African Union authorized the Union of the Comoros government to militarily intervene in Anjouan to restore constitutional order. Comorian forces, with African Union and French support, landed on Anjouan, quickly defeating Bacar's forces. Bacar fled to Réunion (French territory), later extradited to Benin. This military operation successfully ended Anjouan's separation, restoring Union government authority. This was the African Union's first military intervention in a member state, showing the regional organization's determination to maintain constitutional order.

events.title: Mayotte Becomes French Overseas Department Referendum
events.description: Mayotte held a referendum, with 95.2% of voters supporting becoming a French overseas department (département d'outre-mer), enjoying the same status as mainland France. This decision further consolidated Mayotte's integration with France, making it part of the European Union. The Comorian government and African Union strongly protested, considering this a violation of international law and UN resolutions. However, France insisted on respecting Mayotte people's self-determination. The Mayotte issue continued to be a major obstacle in Comoros-France relations.

events.title: Mayotte Officially Becomes French Overseas Department
events.description: Mayotte officially became France's 101st department and fifth overseas department, fully integrated into the French administrative system. Mayotte residents became full EU citizens, enjoying EU law and benefits. This change further widened the gap between Mayotte and other Comorian islands. Mayotte's per capita GDP is far higher than Comoros, attracting large numbers of illegal immigrants from other Comorian islands. The Comorian government continues to claim sovereignty over Mayotte, but is actually powerless to change the status quo.

events.title: Ikililou Elected Union President
events.description: According to the rotation system, candidate from Mohéli island Ikililou Dhoinine was elected Union president. Ikililou was former vice president, known for his moderate and technocratic image. He promised to continue democratic reforms, improve the economy, and strengthen cooperation with the international community. Ikililou's election showed the continued operation of the rotation system, but he faced challenges of economic difficulties, corruption, and political divisions. His term was relatively smooth, without major political crises.

events.title: Constitutional Reform Controversy
events.description: Azali Assoumani ran for president again and pushed for constitutional reform, attempting to abolish the island rotation system for the presidency. Azali claimed the rotation system was inefficient and hindered national development. However, opposition and politicians from Anjouan and Mohéli considered this Azali's plot to extend power and undermine the power balance between islands. Constitutional reform triggered intense political debate and social tensions, threatening the peace framework established by the Fomboni Accord.

events.title: Azali Re-elected President
events.description: Azali Assoumani was re-elected Union president in a controversial election. Opposition alleged electoral fraud and manipulation, but Azali denied the accusations. Azali's victory marked his return to the center of power, and he began pushing his own political agenda, including constitutional reform. Azali's governing style became increasingly authoritarian, suppressing opposition and media freedom. His re-election raised concerns about democratic backsliding in Comoros.

events.title: Constitutional Referendum Abolishes Rotation
events.description: The Azali government held a constitutional referendum, proposing to abolish the island rotation system for the presidency, extend presidential terms, and strengthen presidential powers. Official results showed 92.7% of voters supported the reforms, but turnout was only 63%. Opposition boycotted the referendum, alleging government manipulation of results. Politicians from Anjouan and Mohéli strongly opposed, considering this undermined the core principles of the Fomboni Accord and could trigger new separatist crises. The international community expressed concern about constitutional reform, worrying about Comoros' political stability.

events.title: Azali Re-elected President
events.description: In presidential elections under the new constitutional framework, Azali Assoumani was re-elected with 60.77% of votes. Opposition alleged massive electoral fraud, refused to recognize results, and organized protests. The government suppressed protests, arresting opposition leaders. The African Union and international observers questioned the election's fairness. Azali's re-election consolidated his power but also deepened political divisions and social tensions. Comoros' democratic system faced serious backsliding.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
events.description: The COVID-19 pandemic severely impacted Comoros' fragile economy. Tourism collapsed, diaspora remittances decreased, and government revenue declined. Comoros' already weak healthcare system struggled to cope with the pandemic. The government implemented lockdowns and travel restrictions, but enforcement was poor. International aid helped Comoros respond to the pandemic, but economic recovery was slow. The pandemic exacerbated poverty and unemployment, especially affecting youth and women. Comoros' vaccination rate was low, and the pandemic continued to impact society and economy.

events.title: Political Repression Intensifies
events.description: The Azali government intensified repression of opposition, media, and civil society. Opposition leaders were arrested or exiled, independent media were closed or censored, and protests were violently suppressed. The government used anti-terrorism and national security as pretexts to restrict civil liberties. Human rights organizations criticized Comoros' deteriorating human rights situation, calling for international pressure. However, due to Comoros' low strategic importance, international attention was limited. Political repression deepened social divisions and weakened democratic institutions.

events.title: Economic Difficulties and Debt Crisis
events.description: Comoros faced serious economic difficulties and debt crisis. National debt as a percentage of GDP rose, and fiscal deficits expanded. Comoros heavily depended on foreign aid and diaspora remittances, with limited export income. Vanilla price fluctuations affected major export revenue. Unemployment was high, especially youth unemployment was severe. Infrastructure was backward, and electricity and water supply were unstable. Comoros sought assistance from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, but reform progress was slow. Economic difficulties exacerbated social discontent and political instability.

events.title: Illegal Immigration and Mayotte Crisis
events.description: Comoros and France had tense relations over illegal immigration to Mayotte. Thousands of Comorians risked their lives on makeshift boats (called kwassa-kwassa) to reach Mayotte, seeking better lives. Many died at sea, called the 'largest maritime cemetery in the Indian Ocean.' France strengthened border controls, deporting illegal immigrants, triggering human rights controversies. The Comorian government criticized French immigration policies but was powerless to stop people from leaving. This crisis highlighted the huge economic gap between Comoros and Mayotte and Comoros' development predicament.

events.title: Azali Third Re-election
events.description: Azali Assoumani was elected for a third time in January 2024 presidential elections, with official results showing he received 62.97% of votes. Opposition again alleged massive electoral fraud, including polling station violence, ballot stuffing, and result manipulation. The African Union and international observers expressed serious concerns about the electoral process. Opposition organized protests but faced government repression. Azali's third re-election consolidated his long-term control over Comoros but also raised concerns about authoritarian rule and democratic collapse.

events.title: Contemporary Comoros Challenges
events.description: Comoros remains one of the world's poorest and least developed countries, facing multiple challenges. Politically, authoritarian rule and democratic backsliding threaten political stability, and tensions between islands have intensified due to abolition of the rotation system. Economically, Comoros depends on vanilla exports and diaspora remittances, with limited economic diversification, high unemployment, and backward infrastructure. Socially, rapid population growth (2.2% annual growth rate), high youth population proportion (60% under 25), and weak education and healthcare systems. Environmentally, climate change threatens agriculture and fisheries, and sea level rise threatens coastal communities. The Mayotte issue continues to plague Comoros, with illegal immigration tragedies continuing. Comoros' future depends on achieving political reconciliation, economic development, improved governance, and resolving territorial disputes with France. Despite facing enormous challenges, the Comorian people maintain resilience and hope, working to build a better future.
